item.title: Lil Jon Backs Jay-Z Decision To Book Himself As Super Bowl Pick
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Lil Jon backed Jay-Z's choice to headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show and recalled his own work with Usher.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Jon backed Jay-Z’s decision to book himself for the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show and said he would have done it too.

“I think it’s great for him,” he told Andy Cohen during an appearance on SiriusXM‘s “Andy Cohen Live.”

“Honestly, I probably would have done the same thing. Eventually, I would have pushed myself in there too. I’m not mad at him at all, and I’m sure he’s going to bring out a lot of special guests. He’s already been testing it out in a lot of his shows this year, seeing who he might wanna bring. And he’s already figuring it out,” Lil Jon explained.

He also expected special guests, citing Jay-Z’s recent concerts as a chance to test potential pairings.

Jay-Z will headline the February 14, 2027 show at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The booking puts him in front of the halftime audience after years of helping Roc Nation shape who gets that platform through its work with the NFL.

The company began working with the league in 2019. Recent halftime headliners have included Rihanna, Usher and Kendrick Lamar. Jay-Z has never performed at the Super Bowl, though his concert run this year brought him to SoFi for shows on October 23 and 24.

Lil Jon’s own halftime experience came with Usher in 2024. He told Cohen he served as musical director and performer after directing Usher’s Las Vegas residency. He also thanked Usher for making space for “Turn Down For What” when the singer could have used that time for more of his own songs.

That guest spot involved more than showing up on game day.

“That was an awesome experience too. Not many people can say they were musical director for a Super Bowl halftime as well as performing,” Lil Jon said.

As AllHipHop previously reported, Lil Jon said Justin Bieber had been invited to join Usher’s set but passed before rehearsals began. In explaining that decision, he described a job that required a major commitment of time, practice and preparation for a huge audience.

Bieber still attended the game to support Usher. Onstage, Lil Jon joined Usher and Ludacris for “Yeah!” The set also brought out Alicia Keys, H.E.R., will.i.am and Jermaine Dupri, giving the singer several reunions and guest moments within one halftime performance.

Choosing what to leave out was its own challenge.

In a later appearance on “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” Lil Jon said building Usher’s setlist had been the toughest part. Usher kept revising the selections as the team worked to represent his catalog without disappointing fans. Those changes continued until the end.

item.title: Nelly Recalls Taylor Swift’s $50,000 Favor
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Nelly recalled Taylor Swift offering $50,000 for a Houston performance, with a private flight and a hotel suite for his family.
item.content:encoded:
Nelly said Taylor Swift paid him $50,000 to perform “Hot In Herre” in Houston, and he asked for the cash in a McDonald’s bag.

In his “The Breakfast Club” appearance with Ashanti, as reported by EntertainmentNow, he recalled Swift calling after she and her friends made a dance to the song.

“Sent the G5, not 4, 5,” he told the show, per the outlet.

He said Swift sent a private jet for him and his kids and gave them a presidential suite. His account did not establish the year of the Houston appearance.

Their past shows together also reached beyond that Houston request. On September 29, 2015, Nelly joined Swift onstage in St. Louis during her “1989 World Tour.” They performed “The Fix” before Haim joined them for “Hot In Herre.”

The night marked Haim’s last show as an opening act on that tour. Swift and the sisters danced together during Nelly’s hit. Afterward, Swift shared clips of the routine on social media. Nelly posted footage too, and praised Swift and Haim as his background singers. Haim wore matching white outfits for the number and later compared their look to “Charlie’s Angels” in a social media post.

A different setting brought the two together in August 2016. Swift sang “Dilemma” with Nelly at model Karlie Kloss’ birthday party, as AllHipHop reported at the time. The party performance put Swift in the duet role Kelly Rowland held on the original recording.

Released in 2002, Nelly and Rowland’s “Dilemma” reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The song also won the Grammy for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration.

Now Nelly and Ashanti are giving fans another look at how work fits into their home life. Their series, “Nelly & Ashanti: We Belong Together,” returns to Peacock on November 19.

The second season follows both artists’ careers as they raise their toddler son, Kareem, whom they call KK. Ashanti’s effort to own her master recordings through rerecording her music is part of the story. The couple also weighs whether to share their child on social media while juggling tours in different places.

All eight episodes of the new season will arrive that day.

item.title: SleazyWorld Go Pleads Guilty
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: SleazyWorld Go pleaded guilty to a federal gun charge, prosecutors announced, with sentencing set for January 26, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
SleazyWorld Go pleaded guilty to a federal gun charge, with sentencing set for January 26, 2027, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Kansas.

The October 28 announcement identified him as Joseph R. Isaac, 28, of Kansas City, Kansas. He admitted possessing a firearm as a felon.

A 2016 armed robbery conviction in Michigan barred him from having a gun.

KCTV5’s reporting on court records traced the investigation to an anonymous tip in June 2022. Investigators found more than 30 public social media posts, spread across two years, that showed him with firearms.

Agents tracked his vehicle to a Kansas City, Kansas, townhome complex on October 19, 2022. KCTV5 reported that investigators used binoculars to watch him handle a black pistol. When local police arrived, he and about a dozen associates went into a townhome.

Officers used a phone camera to look through the vehicle’s tinted windows and saw guns inside, according to the court records cited by KCTV5. A search turned up four firearms.

AllHipHop previously covered the March jury verdict, which included a conviction on the felon-in-possession count and an acquittal on the machine gun count.

His management told KCTV5 then that his lawyers planned post-trial motions to address the remaining count. The new announcement did not explain what happened to that verdict or the intervening steps before the plea.

That investigation began during his breakthrough year in music. He grew up in West Michigan before moving to Kansas City, Missouri, and got started with the SleazyWorld collective. His first solo songs arrived in 2020, followed by projects including Big Sleaz and The Sleazy Way. The full-length project Sleazy came out in September 2021.

The 2021 song “Sleazy Flow” became a viral hit. Lil Baby joined the remix in May 2022. That year, he moved from self-released projects to Island Records for Where The Shooters Be, which included “Step 1” with Offset and “Glitches” with G Herbo.

An expanded edition followed in 2023. He also worked with Polo G and Einer Bankz on “Off The Court” before releasing More Than A Shooter in 2024. Skilla Baby and Rob49 appeared on that album.

item.title: Yella Beezy Trial Examines MO3’s Hidden Glock
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Yella Beezy's jury heard how investigators found a concealed Glock in MO3's car during a search nearly three years after his death.
item.content:encoded:
Yella Beezy‘s jury heard Wednesday about a Glock found in MO3’s car nearly three years after his death.

According to FOX 4, ATF agent Derek Wright said a targeted October 18, 2023 search at Dallas police’s impound lot found the pistol. His explosives dog, Chewbacca, alerted near the front passenger seat. Wright said the gun was deliberately hidden and hard to reach.

Crime-scene supervisor Justin O’Donnell said the first search turned up jewelry and $17,960, but no gun. Prosecutors entered the Glock and car photos into evidence.

Yella Beezy, whose legal name is Markies Conway, pleaded not guilty to capital murder. Prosecutors accused him of paying Kewon White $40,000 to kill MO3 after a feud that began in 2017.

His lawyers disputed both the alleged payment and the state’s explanation of the money. They argued that cash White had came from drug activity, rather than from Yella Beezy.

Defense lawyer Toby Shook told jurors the state would ask them to fill holes in its case with assumptions. He urged them to watch for reasonable doubt as witnesses testified. The defense’s account put the source of White’s cash at the center of the fight over whether the killing was paid for.

The separate trial of White ended in September with a capital murder conviction and a sentence of life without parole. MO3, whose legal name was Melvin Noble, was killed on Interstate 35E in Dallas on November 11, 2020.

Before Yella Beezy’s trial, his lawyers sought more time to prepare after White’s case. The defense wanted transcripts so it could check what witnesses said in the first trial against their accounts before a new jury.

The lawyers also wanted expert Julianna Moore available. Her background included 18 years of work in the federal court system. His lawyers wanted her to explain benefits that witnesses in related federal drug cases could receive for helping prosecutors.

The witness lists in the two cases were nearly the same: prosecutors listed 264 people in Yella Beezy’s case and 263 in White’s. That overlap gave the earlier testimony a direct role in the defense’s preparation.

Testimony was set to resume Thursday at 9 a.m.

item.title: Neurosurgeon Describes Witnessing MO3’s Fatal Shooting in Yella Beezy Murder Trial
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: A neurosurgeon who witnessed MO3's fatal shooting on I-35 testified Wednesday in Yella Beezy's murder-for-hire trial, describing the violence in detail.
item.content:encoded:
A neurosurgeon who witnessed the fatal shooting of MO3 on Interstate 35 provided harrowing testimony Wednesday in the murder-for-hire trial of Dallas rapper Yella Beezy.

Dr. Randall Graham, a brain and spine surgeon at Methodist Health System, was commuting between two Dallas hospitals when he became an eyewitness to the November 2020 killing.

Graham was driving northbound on I-35 around noon when traffic suddenly slowed to a standstill.

“I remember it was around noon and in 2020 there was quite a bit of construction going on on the highway at that time and that portion of highway is built as is almost like a big overpass where there’s no shoulders. Uh there are guard rails that come by to the lanes at least at that time. Uh that’s what it look like. And so around noon um as I was heading north traffic slowed down to essentially a standill uh which was unusual for that time of day and that day of week um but I thought with construction maybe there was some type of construction related delay at first.”

What happened next unfolded in seconds. Graham heard repeated loud banging noises before seeing a Black male sprinting toward his vehicle on the passenger side.

Moments later, he heard and felt what he described as an explosion. Glass and debris sprayed across his face and neck. A bullet had pierced his windshield.

A second man followed, this one carrying what appeared to be a rifle. The shooter stood near Graham’s passenger-side headlight and fired two or three shots before walking away. Graham immediately realized he’d been shot at and feared for his life.

“I noticed a bullet hole in my windshield. And so I sort of connected that what happened was a bullet flew through my windshield. I think the first thing that went through my head was I thought that my life would probably end that day.”

Graham called 911 while still in his vehicle, describing the active shooting to the dispatcher.

“The first thing I did was I called 911 while I was in the car and I spoke to the dispatcher and described that there was an active shooting occurring on on I described my location as best as I could. And then after um I disconnected with with 911 I pulled my vehicle forward and to the right towards towards the right side right and stop my vehicle there at that point.”

When he exited his car, a group of Hispanic women were screaming in Spanish and pointing to a victim lying on the highway.

Despite being a neurosurgeon rather than a trauma specialist, Graham sprang into action.

“I approached the victim and uh I started doing chest compressions and CPR. I noticed he was still breathing. They weren’t normal breaths. There’s quite a bit of blood. I did notice he had multiple multiple gunshot wounds., So, you know, I did what I thought was best and tried to revive him as best as I could.”

The victim, later identified as MO3, was exhibiting what Graham described as agonal respirations, a critical medical sign.

“Agonal breathing is an involuntary reflex. It looks like someone is irregularly rolled in air and it’s it’s not normal breathing. It’s not actually getting oxygen into the lungs effectively the way that you’re breathing out. And the reason it occurs is when there’s been so much injury or damage to the brain that the very basic respiratory centers of the brain are actually injured and triggering these abnormal breaths in sort of the last ditch attempt to oxygenate the tissues in the body.”

Graham performed CPR for approximately 25 minutes before first responders arrived.

Despite his efforts and medical expertise, the injuries were too severe.

Graham later explained that in his career, he had never seen a patient with such injuries survive, even with immediate hospital care.

The shooting occurred during the commission of a murder-for-hire plot.

Yella Beezy is Markies Conway, is accused of hiring and paying Kewon White to kill MO3.

White was convicted of capital murder in September and sentenced to life without parole. Conway has pleaded not guilty.

A third defendant, Devin Brown Jr., is awaiting trial.

Graham’s injuries from the shooting were treated at the hospital where he worked.

He had glass embedded in his neck and a bullet hole in his windshield, while a large piece of the projectile was later removed from his sun visor.

His testimony provided the jury with a detailed, firsthand account of the violence that claimed MO3’s life.

item.title: Nicki Minaj Calls Kathy Hochul An “Evil Woman”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Nicki Minaj called Kathy Hochul an evil woman and backed Bruce Blakeman, while the governor blamed the rapper's Trump rallies.
item.content:encoded:
Nicki Minaj called Kathy Hochul an “evil woman” Wednesday (October 28). She predicted divine punishment for Hochul.

Governor Hochul’s told people to “get outside, and stop going to Trump rallies, it’s kind of poisoning your mind.”

Nicki Minaj fired back and urged Black and Christian voters to support Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, citing Hochul’s old comments about Black children and computers.

Blakeman praised Minaj and joked about a moving truck for Hochul.

Minaj’s criticism returned attention to a remark that drew 50 Cent’s criticism in May 2024. Hochul had said young Black children in the Bronx did not know what a computer was while speaking at the Milken Institute Global Conference in California.

In that earlier dispute, 50 Cent questioned the idea that children in the Bronx were unfamiliar with computers and pointed to their skill with iPads.

The governor was discussing the state’s Empire AI Consortium and the opportunities she hoped it would create. Her comments came on May 6, 2024, more than two years before Minaj’s latest posts.

Hochul apologized later that same day. She said she had misspoken, acknowledged that Black children in the Bronx knew what computers were and said the problem was access to technology that could help them reach well-paid jobs in fields such as artificial intelligence.

Trump’s influence was already a point of conflict in the governor’s race. At a Sunday campaign stop at Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn, Hochul criticized Blakeman’s support for the president, WABC reported. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined her to rally union members. It was his second campaign appearance with Hochul in three days.

Blakeman, meanwhile, campaigned in Yorktown Heights with former Westchester County Executive Rob Astorino. He attacked Hochul’s alliance with Mamdani as the candidates sought votes in the final stretch.

Trump endorsed Blakeman’s campaign, according to FOX 5 New York‘s account of the candidates’ backers. Hochul’s supporters included Mamdani, Attorney General Letitia James and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

New York’s early voting period runs through November 1. Election Day is November 3, with polls open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., according to the state Board of Elections. Early voting hours vary from county to county.

item.title: Dame Dash Questions $550K Life-Rights Bid: “I’m Flattered”
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Dame Dash questioned the $550,000 winning bid for his life rights, calling the interest flattering as a longtime legal rival joined in.
item.content:encoded:
Dame Dash called interest in his life story flattering while questioning the $550,000 winning bid at his bankruptcy auction.

Speaking in an interview posted by The Art Of Dialogue on October 28, Dash challenged the idea that a public figure’s life could carry that price.

“I’ve never heard of anything like that,” he said.

His response followed an October 1 bankruptcy auction, where Everlasting Films LLC beat a $500,000 backup bid from Doug Peters, according to the trustee’s notice.

Dash argued that filmmakers could already tell stories about public figures, citing documentaries and movies about Sean Combs and Donald Trump to explain his view.

“So if somebody pays for my life rights, which from what I understand, life rights are free, you know, like there was a documentary made about Puff that I’m sure he didn’t get paid for. Donald Trump has a lot of movies made about him on Netflix. Like once you’re a public figure, it’s public domain.”

He also said he saw the interest in his story as a compliment, while questioning whether such a deal could withstand a constitutional challenge.

“I’m flattered that my life rights mean so much. I’m flattered that the intention is to make a movie about me that must have a bigger budget than the life rights unless they’re dumb. I’m flattered that now I get to really fight for something that if it did happen would appear to be unconstitutional.”

The auction also involved someone Dash had fought in court: attorney Christopher Brown, who participated in the bid with Everlasting.

Brown won a December 2022 defamation case that left Dash and his company Poppington owing $50,000 each. The attorney also represented filmmaker Josh Webber in his efforts to collect money from Dash after winning judgments.

Dash previously pointed to Brown’s collection efforts when explaining his bankruptcy decision during a September 2025 appearance on The Breakfast Club.

Dash sought Chapter 7 protection in Florida on September 4, 2025, listing $25.3 million in debt and $4,350 in personal assets.

He reported no monthly income as taxes, child support and court judgments accounted for the debts he sought relief from.

New York State had already bought his one-third Roc-A-Fella share for $1 million in November 2024 toward nearly $9 million in unpaid taxes.

The trustee’s terms gave Everlasting 10 days after entry of a sale order to close the deal.

item.title: Rod Wave Adds Abdou Toure To Mainstay Sports
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Rod Wave added Arkansas freshman Abdou Toure to Mainstay Sports Agency as the rapper expanded his business beyond music.
item.content:encoded:
Rod Wave added Arkansas freshman Abdou Toure to Mainstay Sports Agency on Wednesday, bringing a top basketball prospect into his growing business outside music.

On3 reported the signing and cited a statement Rod Wave gave ESPN about his new client. “I believe he’s a superstar talent, and a superstar person,” he said.

The deal covers marketing and brand representation, according to the New Haven Register. Mainstay Sports launched in August. Its clients include Olympic medalist Will Claye, Kendrick Perkins’ son Kenxton Perkins and Houston commit Oneal Delancy. The sports firm sits under the same Mainstay umbrella as a touring division.

Toure already had a foothold in the merchandise business. New Haven’s Goatville Apparel introduced a Toure Collection last year, the newspaper reported. He also had about 60,000 followers on TikTok.

The 6-foot-5 guard came to Arkansas from Notre Dame High School in West Haven, Connecticut. The school’s official biography lists him as the Allen Iverson High School Player of the Year and a five-star recruit across the major recruiting services. He also represented Guinea on the Nike Hoop Summit World Team.

His profile had grown well beyond his home state before college. Toure played for Guinea at the 2024 FIBA U17 World Cup and appeared in the Iverson Classic and BallisLife All-American games. Arkansas also lists second-team All-American honors from MaxPreps and the Naismith Awards in 2026.

For Rod Wave, Mainstay already has work across several parts of entertainment. As AllHipHop previously reported, Mainstay Touring produced his “Don’t Look Down Tour”. The original announcement billed that run as a 25-city trip across North America, with Fridayy as the special guest. It included stops in Houston, Dallas, Los Angeles and Brooklyn.

The Mainstay name also appeared behind the camera. A tour announcement from Philadelphia’s Xfinity Mobile Arena said Rod Wave’s own company, Mainstay Films, produced the trailer for Don’t Look Down. Rod Wave starred in the trailer himself.

That announcement described Don’t Look Down as his seventh full-length album and the follow-up to Last Lap. The 2024 album opened at No. 2 on the Billboard 200 and gave him a fifth straight top-three entry, the venue said.

item.title: Argentina’s “Big N#gga Burgers” Is Not A Vibe With Racial & Hip-Hop Implications
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: An Argentine burger restaurant called Big Nigga Burgers is drawing international criticism over its racially charged name.
item.content:encoded:
Big Nigga Burgers.

Read that three time. This place has become an international controversy after an Argentine restaurant’s unusual, presumably racist name caught the attention of America. And somehow they credit Hip-Hop culture for the inspiration.

Yes, ladies and gentlemen, somebody actually named a burger joint “Big Nigga Burgers.” And apparently, the owners are surprised that people have something to say about it.

The establishment is located in Llavallol, Buenos Aires, Argentina and owned by Jackie and Franco. The all started around 2020. Their specialty? Smash burgers featuring black buns, double beef patties, cheddar cheese, bacon and red onions.

Sounds delicious to some. I’d never eat that. And the name is giving people indigestion.

The restaurant reportedly embraces Hip-Hop and trap music as part of its identity, but I have not completely been able to verify that. I definitely do not excuse that. Is that cultural appreciation? I don’t think we want it. Or do we?

As images and videos of the establishment circulated online, American social media users began questioning why a restaurant in Argentina would casually incorporate one of the most historically offensive words in the world into its business name.

The owners have defended their branding, explaining that the name was inspired by rap music and designed to attract attention rather than offend anyone.

“We’re just another damn burger joint in this world, but call it luck or coincidence, today there’s something that sets us apart and brings people from all over the world,” one of the owners said.

They definitely have that Argentine spirit…they don’t give a damn.

Jackie and Franco wrote:

“We won’t change or make ourselves smaller just to fit in. We know who we are.”

They continued:

“And to those who insult us or hope to see us fail: you don’t have to like us, but you’ll never stop us.”

And finished with:

“This is who we are. Jackie and Franco. Big Nigga Burgers, we’re only getting started.”

OK.

Hip-Hop is mainstream. It has traveled around the world, influencing everything from fashion and language to food and entrepreneurship. Argentina has its own Hip-Hop community, and nobody is suggesting that the country cannot participate in the culture. However, is this how y’all show appreciation.

The N-word carries centuries of racial trauma, even though some Black artists have reclaimed variations of it within specific cultural contexts. The business trivializes anti-Black racism, while the owners maintain that their intentions were never malicious.

There is some history here, y’all!

Argentina has a troubling history of anti-Black racism, including 19th-century efforts to promote European immigration, suppress Afro-Argentine identity and effectively erase Black people from the nation’s historical narrative, making the restaurant’s controversial name particularly ironic.Anti-Black racism remains a documented problem in Argentina in 2026, although its manifestations can differ from those in the United States.

Afro-Argentines continue to report racial discrimination, stereotyping, unequal treatment and the marginalization of Black people in the country’s media, institutions and historical narrative.This is 2026. I will not go farther. I know y’all don’t read this much and Chat is a pretty good friend.

For now, the restaurant has accomplished something many small businesses can only dream about. It has people around the world discussing its name. In a most disgusting way…and yet, if racism is regular and supported there…they’ll fare well.

And I’m left wondering one thing.

Would you eat there?

item.title: Ja Rule Named IPX Celebrity Board President
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ja Rule became president of IPX's celebrity advisory board and a founding shareholder, with a role in creator ownership.
item.content:encoded:
Ja Rule became president of IPX’s celebrity board of advisors and a founding shareholder, adding a stake in a company that said it would help artists keep control of their work.

The company said he would help shape how artists, athletes and creators retain rights and how their projects get funded and made.

“I’m a creative first, and I’ve seen firsthand what can happen to artists who don’t own their work. When I create IP, I make sure every show is my IP, on purpose, so that content will be ours, forever. That’s why IPX is a game-changer for the industry, empowering celebrities, creatives and fans alike. We’re rewriting the script on how celebrities own and retain their IP,” Ja Rule told AllHipHop.com in a statement.

On its website, IPX described production tools for budgets, casting, crew schedules and records of who holds a project’s rights.

It also listed podcast production and distribution services, alongside live broadcasts. For sponsors, the company outlined a system that would hold payment until agreed campaign goals were met. It listed audience reach and event attendance among those goals.

The fan side had a different entry point. IPX advertised production memberships starting at $100, with access to content, experiences and other perks. Its website said members who helped through testing, feedback or promotion might receive payments.

It also said any financial benefit was uncertain and depended on factors including the member’s active work.

The new appointment followed another business Ja Rule helped build from an investment into a product.

In an interview with Food & Wine, he traced Amber & Opal to whiskey barrels he and his partners initially bought to age and sell. They later created their own brand, which launched in Maryland in 2024.

He has since dealt with the staffing demands of that ownership.

As AllHipHop previously reported, the whiskey’s four founders held off on a wider store rollout to concentrate on seven markets they could visit and support.

Ja Rule told Inc. the brand could enter 238 stores, but the team wanted more help before expanding. Co-founder Herb Rice explained that getting bottles into stores was only part of the job.

The founders also needed to keep visiting bars and retailers to help sell the product. The team sought $5 million to $7 million to hire staff and support its next markets.
